questions.questionText:
First 6 successive ionisation energies (kJ/mol) of Period 3 element X are: 786, 1580, 3230, 4360, 16100, 19800.
(a) State which group of the Periodic Table X belongs to and explain your reasoning. [3 marks]
(b) Explain why first ionisation energy drops slightly between Mg and Al. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Group 14 (IV) [1]. Huge jump occurs between IE₄ (4,360) and IE₅ (16,100), showing 4 outer-shell valence electrons; removing the 5th breaks into a stable inner shell closer to the nucleus [2].
(b) Al's outer electron is in a higher-energy 3p orbital further from nucleus and shielded by 3s² electrons, so less energy removes it than Mg's 3s electron [3].

questions.questionText:
Hess's Law & Enthalpy Cycles:
Given standard enthalpies of combustion (kJ/mol): C(s) = -394, H₂(g) = -286, CH₃OH(l) = -726.
Construct an enthalpy cycle and calculate ΔH°_f of liquid methanol CH₃OH(l). [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
C(s) + 2H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → CH₃OH(l).
ΔH°_f = ΣΔH°_c(reactants) - ΔH°_c(product) = [-394 + 2(-286)] - (-726) = -966 + 726 = -240 kJ/mol [4 marks].

questions.questionText:
Chemical Equilibria (Kp):
For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), 1.00 mol of N₂O₄ dissociates in a vessel at 120°C and total equilibrium pressure 200 kPa until 60% has dissociated.
(a) Write the Kp expression. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate partial pressures and the numerical value of Kp with units. [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Kp = p(NO₂)² / p(N₂O₄) [1].
(b) Initial moles N₂O₄ = 1.00; dissociated = 0.60 -> remaining N₂O₄ = 0.40 mol, formed NO₂ = 1.20 mol. Total equilibrium moles = 1.60 [2]. p(N₂O₄) = (0.40/1.60)×200 = 50 kPa; p(NO₂) = (1.20/1.60)×200 = 150 kPa [2]. Kp = 150² / 50 = 450 kPa [1].

questions.questionText:
Reaction Kinetics:
For 2NO(g) + H₂(g) → N₂O(g) + H₂O(g), doubling [NO] quadruples rate, while doubling [H₂] doubles rate.
(a) Write the rate equation and state overall order. [2 marks]
(b) Given initial rate = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol/(dm³·s) when [NO] = 0.020 and [H₂] = 0.015 mol/dm³, calculate rate constant k with units. [3 marks]

Buffer Solutions & pH:
(a) Explain how an ethanoic acid / sodium ethanoate buffer resists sharp pH change when small amounts of H⁺ or OH⁻ are added, using equations. [4 marks]
(b) Calculate the pH of a buffer containing 0.20 mol/dm³ CH₃COOH (Ka = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵) and 0.40 mol/dm³ CH₃COONa. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻. Added H⁺ reacts with large reserve of CH₃COO⁻ forming weak undissociated CH₃COOH; added OH⁻ reacts with H⁺, shifting CH₃COOH dissociation right to restore H⁺ [4].
(b) [H⁺] = Ka([Acid]/[Salt]) = 1.7×10⁻⁵ × (0.20/0.40) = 8.5×10⁻⁶ mol/dm³. pH = -log₁₀(8.5×10⁻⁶) = 5.07 [3].

questions.questionText:
Born–Haber Cycle for MgO:
Define "Lattice Energy" and explain why the lattice enthalpy of MgO (-3,791 kJ/mol) is much more exothermic than that of NaCl (-787 kJ/mol). [4 marks]
questions.explanation: Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of solid ionic lattice is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions [2]. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry doubly charged ions (2+ / 2−) and smaller ionic radii than Na⁺/Cl⁻, producing far stronger electrostatic attraction [2].

questions.questionText:
Electrochemistry (Standard Electrode Potentials):
Given E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = -0.76 V:
(a) Write the overall cell diagram and balanced equation for the feasible Daniell cell. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate E°_cell and state the direction of electron flow in the external circuit. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s); Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) [2].
(b) E°_cell = +0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V; electrons flow through wire from Zinc anode to Copper cathode [3].

questions.questionText:
Period 3 Oxides & Chlorides:
Explain why Na₂O forms a strongly alkaline solution (pH 13) in water, Al₂O₃ is amphoteric and insoluble, and SiCl₄ hydrolyses violently giving misty fumes. Include balanced equations. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Na₂O is ionic with O²⁻ ions that react vigorously with water: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH (pH 13) [2]. Al₂O₃ has strong lattice + partial covalent character making it insoluble, reacting with both acids (Al₂O₃ + 6H⁺ → 2Al³⁺ + 3H₂O) and hot alkalis (Al₂O₃ + 2OH⁻ + 3H₂O → 2[Al(OH)₄]⁻) [2]. SiCl₄ has empty 3d orbitals allowing nucleophilic water attack: SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl(g) misty fumes [2].

questions.questionText:
Transition Metals:
(a) Explain why transition elements show variable oxidation states and form coloured aqueous complexes using d-orbital splitting. [4 marks]
(b) Explain why ligand exchange from [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ to [CuCl₄]²⁻ changes both colour and coordination number. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Small energy gap between 3d and 4s subshells allows losing varying numbers of electrons [2]. Ligands split degenerate 3d orbitals into ΔE gaps; d-d electron transitions absorb specific visible wavelengths leaving the complementary colour transmitted [2].
(b) Pale blue octahedral [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (coord 6) turns yellow-green tetrahedral [CuCl₄]²⁻ (coord 4) because larger Cl⁻ ligands limit 4 around Cu²⁺ and alter ΔE [3].

questions.questionText:
Organic Mechanisms (Nucleophilic Substitution SN1 vs SN2):
Compare the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with the SN2 hydrolysis of bromoethane in terms of rate equation, stereochemistry, and carbocation stability. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: SN1 (tertiary): Rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr] (first-order), forms a planar carbocation stabilised by three electron-donating methyl groups (+I effect), leading to racemic mixture if chiral [3]. SN2 (primary): Rate = k[CH₃CH₂Br][OH⁻] (second-order), concerted backside attack via 5-coordinate transition state giving clean Walden inversion of configuration [3].

questions.questionText:
Electrophilic Substitution of Benzene vs Phenol:
Why does phenol react instantaneously with aqueous bromine at room temperature to form white 2,4,6-tribromophenol, whereas benzene requires an AlBr₃/FeBr₃ catalyst and warming? [5 marks]
questions.explanation: In phenol, a lone pair on oxygen overlaps into the delocalised benzene π-ring, greatly increasing ring electron density and activating positions 2, 4, and 6 [3]. This polarises Br₂ directly without a halogen-carrier Lewis acid catalyst, forming 2,4,6-tribromophenol white precipitate + 3HBr [2].

questions.questionText:
Carbonyl Chemistry & Mechanisms:
Outline the nucleophilic addition mechanism of HCN (with KCN catalyst) to propanone (CH₃COCH₃) to form 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile, explaining why racemic mixtures form from asymmetric ketones. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Step 1: :CN⁻ attacks δ⁺ carbonyl C, pushing π-bond electrons onto O⁻ [2]. Step 2: Alkoxide O⁻ abstracts H⁺ from HCN regenerating CN⁻ catalyst [1]. Since carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar, CN⁻ attacks equally from above or below, giving a 50:50 optically inactive racemic mixture [2].

questions.questionText:
Carboxylic Acids, Acyl Chlorides & Esters:
Compare the relative ease of hydrolysis of chloroethane, chlorobenzene, and ethanoyl chloride with cold water, giving structural explanations. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Ethanoyl chloride (CH₃COCl) hydrolyses instantaneously/violently in cold water because carbonyl C is bonded to two strongly electronegative atoms (O and Cl), creating large δ⁺ for fast water attack [2]. Chloroethane reacts slowly on warming [1.5]. Chlorobenzene resists hydrolysis because C-Cl lone pair delocalises into the π-ring strengthening the bond [1.5].

questions.questionText:
Amines, Diazonium Salts & Azo Dyes:
Describe the two-step synthesis of a brightly coloured azo dye starting from phenylamine (aniline), stating reagents, temperature control (<10°C), and coupling phenol in NaOH. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Step 1 (Diazotisation): React phenylamine with NaNO₂ + dilute HCl kept below 5–10°C (using ice bath; above 10°C it decomposes to phenol + N₂) forming benzenediazonium chloride [C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻] [3]. Step 2 (Coupling): Pour cold diazonium salt into alkaline phenol (dissolved in cold NaOH) to yield orange-red azo dye via -N=N- bridge [2].

questions.questionText:
Polymerisation & Amino Acids:
(a) Explain what a zwitterion is using glycine (H₂NCH₂COOH) and explain why amino acids have high melting points and dissolve in water. [3 marks]
(b) Distinguish addition polymerisation (polythene) from condensation polymerisation (nylon-6,6 / Terylene). [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Zwitterion is a neutral dipolar ion ⁺H₃NCH₂COO⁻ formed by internal proton transfer; strong ionic lattice attractions give high melting points and hydration in water [3].
(b) Addition links unsaturated alkene monomers with 100% atom economy (no small byproduct); condensation links bifunctional monomers (diamine + dicarboxylic acid / diol) eliminating small molecules like H₂O or HCl [3].

questions.questionText:
Entropy & Gibbs Free Energy (ΔG = ΔH - TΔS):
For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +178 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +161 J/(K·mol).
(a) Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and state whether decomposition is spontaneous. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the minimum temperature (in K and °C) above which thermal decomposition becomes spontaneous. [2 marks]

Analytical Chemistry — Mass Spectrometry & ¹H NMR:
State how high-resolution mass spectrometry and ¹H NMR (chemical shift δ and n+1 splitting rule) distinguish ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) from methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃). [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Same molecular formula C₂H₆O -> identical M⁺ peak at m/z 46, but fragmentation shows m/z 31 (CH₂OH⁺) & 45 for ethanol vs m/z 15/45 for ether [2]. In ¹H NMR: methoxymethane gives just ONE singlet peak (6 equivalent H); ethanol gives THREE peaks — triplet (CH₃), quartet (CH₂), and broad singlet (OH) [3].

questions.questionText:
Group 2 Thermal Stability:
Explain why the thermal decomposition temperatures of Group 2 carbonates and nitrates increase down the group from Mg to Ba. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: Cation ionic radius increases down Group 2 (Mg²⁺ → Ba²⁺) while charge stays +2, so charge density and polarising power decrease [2]. Larger cations distort the electron cloud of the large CO₃²⁻/NO₃⁻ anion much less, requiring higher temperature to decompose the bond [2].

questions.questionText:
Redox Titration (KMnO₄ vs Fe²⁺):
25.0 cm³ of acidified FeSO₄(aq) required 22.50 cm³ of 0.0200 mol/dm³ KMnO₄(aq) for oxidation.
(a) Write the balanced ionic equation. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the concentration of Fe²⁺(aq) in mol/dm³. [3 marks]

Solubility Product (Ksp) & Common Ion Effect:
Lead(II) chloride has Ksp = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ mol³·dm⁻⁹ at 25°C.
(a) Calculate the molar solubility of PbCl₂ in pure water. [3 marks]
(b) Explain qualitatively how adding NaCl(aq) affects PbCl₂ solubility. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) PbCl₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ -> Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³ -> s³ = 4.0×10⁻⁶ -> s = 0.0159 mol/dm³ [3].
(b) Extra Cl⁻ increases [Cl⁻] (common ion effect), shifting equilibrium left to precipitate PbCl₂ so solubility drops sharply [2].
